catalog_quote: 2.1.2 Tone. Suprasegmentally, a three- or four-way contrast in pitch is present on monosyllables in all languages—High (H), Low (L), and Fall (HL)—so it seems reasonable to posit at least these tonal contrasts in the protolanguage. ... Finally, despite the three-way contrast on monosyllables, Skou at least of the Skou family shows a five-way contrast in tone at the word level (see Donohue 1997 for a discussion of the tone patterns found in New Guinea), with a partial collapse of distinctions in monosyllables. ... [p.180] Leitre verbs have the typical syllable structure of the language, (C)V(T)(±N), showing a contrast in nasalization. ... [p.181] The original HL tone melody is preserved, being realized as an F tone on the languages that exhibit reduction. (This is some support for the notion that the tonal system of the Skou languages is, like Skou itself, a word-tone system [Donohue 1997], not a syllable-tone one).

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (51 pp., text layer, published running heads 'oceanic linguistics, vol. 41, no. 1' / pagination 171-221; extracted text PDF pp.7-11 = pp.177-181). The quote is verbatim in two pieces: (a) PDF p.9 = p.179, opening of sec. 2.1.2: 'Tone. Suprasegmentally, a three- or four-way contrast in pitch is present on monosyllables in all languages—High (H), Low (L), and Fall (HL)—so it seems reasonable to posit at least these tonal contrasts in the protolanguage.9' (footnote marker 9 dropped in the reader's quote); (b) PDF p.11 = p.181: '(This is some support for the notion that the tonal system of the Skou languages is, like Skou itself, a word-tone system [Donohue 1997], not a syllable-tone one…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Leitre is a word-tone language: every monosyllable carries one of three or four contrastive pitches (Donohue 2002 p.179: H, L, HL for all six Skou-family languages; Donohue & Crowther 2005 Table 4 p.182 give Leitre specifically H, L, F, Rf plus contrastive nasalisation; Donohue 2003 Table 8 p.360 gives Leitre pitches 4553, 22, 52, 354), and tone melodies belong to the word/morpheme, not the syllable. No source examined says anything about word stress in Leitre, so no stress position can be recorded; the Skou grammar's family table (Donohue 2004 Table 8 p.22) leaves the 'Stress' row blank while entering 'tonal, nasalisation' under Tone.
new_statements.exceptions: None; Donohue 2002 p.179 warns that tone correspondences are complex and that pitch data from survey-only languages (Leitre was surveyed by Donohue in 2000) are 'less sure'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word/morpheme-level tone (word-tone system); data from citation forms in comparative wordlists (Donohue 2004 Appendix 5 marks Leitre words with H/L/F/R pitch letters). The statement is a family-wide one covering Leitre explicitly among the six languages of Table 1; the Leitre-specific tone inventory is only tabulated (Donohue & Crowther 2005; Donohue 2003).
new_statements.identity_note: Leitre [leit1234], spoken in Leitre (Laitre) village on the coast east of Vanimo, Sandaun Province; no ISO code (Glottolog NOCODE_Leitre), absent from Ethnologue E16-E28; ASJP files its two wordlists (LEITRE = Donohue, LEITRE_2 = Dryer 2019) under Vanimo [vam]/vani1248, but Glottolog (on Donohue 2002 and p.c. Dryer 2022) treats it as a language distinct from Vanimo/Dumo/Dusur. All statements here come from Donohue's own 2000 survey data on Leitre village.
